title: Mara and the Letter
premise: In 1893, on a storm-battered island off the Cornish coast, widowed lighthouse keeper Coral Ashgrove has spent seven years hiding her late husband's role in a smuggling ring that drowned four men — and hiding her brother-in-law, a fugitive living in the lighthouse cellar. When census taker Edmund Vane arrives to document every soul on the island, his questions threaten to expose them all, and Coral must decide whether silence or truth will keep her family alive. As the great storms close in, a government ship offers one berth of escape before the morning tide, forcing Coral to choose between her daughter, her brother-in-law, and herself. In the end she gives up her own place, stays to keep the light burning through the worst night of the century, and finds that justice — and love — can survive outside the law.
about_author: C. M. Underhill is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing lighthouse keepers' logs along the Atlantic coast. Their fiction draws on the unspoken bargains small coastal communities made with the sea and with the law.

chapters.title: The Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. During the annual census, Edmund Vane asks how many souls dwell at the light — and Coral hesitates one beat too long over 'four.' The chapter establishes her careful silences and ends with Edmund noticing the extra bowl drying by the sink. Emotional beat: dread beneath routine.

chapters.title: What the Cellar Keeps
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Flashback woven through present: her brother-in-law Tobias has hidden below for two years since the wreck that killed four smugglers, including her husband's accomplices. Her daughter Wren believes he's a ghost story. Beat: the weight of protective lies.

chapters.title: A Man Who Counts Things
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Lodging at the island inn, Edmund reviews his forms and finds Coral's household arithmetic wrong by one. A meticulous, lonely man, he tells himself it's only accuracy he wants. Beat: curiosity hardening into obligation.

chapters.title: Wren Counts Stars
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, age eleven. She knows more than her mother thinks — she's seen the cellar door open at night and heard a man coughing. She begins leaving bread on the stairs. Beat: a child's loyalty forming in secret.

chapters.title: The First Great Storm
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The season's first killer gale strikes; Coral keeps the light alone through the night while Tobias, breaking cover to help, nearly reveals himself to a rescued fisherman. Beat: competence as armor, cracks showing.

chapters.title: Ledgers and Wrecks
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. In the harbor office he finds the old inquiry file on the smuggling wreck — names redacted, but the Ashgrove surname circled. He realizes the dead men were never all accounted for. Beat: the past surfacing like flotsam.

chapters.title: Bread on the Stairs
chapters.summary: Tobias's POV. From the dark of the cellar, Tobias narrates his guilt over the drowned men and his growing tenderness toward Wren, whom he watches from the stair shadows. He decides to surrender rather than endanger them. Beat: guilt turning toward sacrifice.

chapters.title: An Offer of Passage
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The revenue cutter Meridian arrives ahead of the storm season's end: authorities suspect a fugitive on the island and offer any resident claiming fear a berth on the mainland sailing at morning tide. Coral understands it's a trap dressed as mercy. Beat: hope sharpened into menace.

chapters.title: Edmund Comes Back
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Edmund returns to correct the census and finds Wren alone; she lets slip that 'Uncle Toby' taught her knots. Instead of reporting it, he walks back down the cliff path without writing a word. Beat: duty beginning to bend.

chapters.title: The Bargain at the Harbor
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Coral confronts the cutter's captain, offering information about the smuggling ring's surviving financier in exchange for Tobias's safe passage — if she can name him before the tide. Beat: love negotiating with law.

chapters.title: What Silences Cost
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Edmund confronts Coral privately: he knows about the fourth man in her household. She asks what he'll do with what he counts. He admits he no longer knows whether accuracy is the same as truth. Beat: two keepers of secrets recognizing each other.

chapters.title: The Financier's Name
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Coral finally speaks her husband's deepest secret aloud: the ring was funded by the island's beloved harbormaster, who let the four men drown to erase debts. Naming him means ruining the community that sheltered her. Beat: the price of justice made concrete.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Barometers fall; the great storm of the year bears down. Wren, sent to warn Tobias, finally meets him face to face in the cellar and chooses not to be afraid. Beat: family defined by choice, not blood.

chapters.title: The Harbormaster Moves
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. The harbormaster, tipped off, accuses Edmund of falsifying the census and demands the cutter search the lighthouse immediately — tonight, in rising seas. Beat: the net closing from both sides.

chapters.title: One Berth
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The captain, moved by Coral's testimony but bound by orders, can protect only one person from prosecution when the search comes: a single berth on the morning-tide boat. Coral must choose between Tobias and Wren. Beat: the blurb's terrible choice arriving.

chapters.title: The Choice
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, night. Coral decides Wren will sail to safety with papers naming her ward of the Underhill cousins on the mainland; Tobias refuses to take a child's place until Wren herself argues she can carry their story where his cannot go. Beat: grief and resolve entwined.

chapters.title: The Worst Night of the Century
chapters.summary: Alternating Coral and Edmund. The storm hits full force as the search party climbs to the light; Coral keeps the lamp burning while Edmund, inside the party, miscounts heads in the dark — deliberately. Beat: climax; courage and quiet treason under wind.

chapters.title: Light Against Water
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. A ship founders on the rocks; Coral and Tobias work the winches together to save survivors, including the harbormaster's own son. The rescue makes prosecution of the Ashgroves politically impossible. Beat: salvation through the very act they hid.

chapters.title: Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. At dawn Wren boards the boat alone, clutching Tobias's compass and her mother's promise. She watches the lighthouse shrink and does not cry until the island is gone. Beat: heartbreak braided with hope.

chapters.title: The Reckoning
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Edmund files his true census — four souls, then three — and submits evidence against the harbormaster, ending his own career. Justice arrives outside any courtroom: the community itself turns the harbormaster out. Beat: cost accepted, integrity kept.

chapters.title: After the Storms
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Spring comes; the board of trade, embarrassed by the harbormaster affair, grants Coral a formal commendation and Tobias a pardon for service rendered. The house feels too big by one voice. Beat: survival's hollow ache and its quiet grace.

chapters.title: The Letter
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, final chapter. A letter arrives from Wren — thriving, learning knots from new hands — with a pressed starflower inside. Coral reads it in the lantern room, lights the lamp, and for the first time in seven years says a name out loud: her husband's, forgiven. Beat: peace earned, silences finally chosen rather than forced.
